problems.description: Any client can send a 'system'-type message and have it broadcast to all peers, spoofing authoritative server messages (the server's own 'connected' notice uses the same shape). System messages should be server-issued only, not accepted from clients.

_is_valid_message requires a client-supplied 'timestamp' string, but the server immediately overwrites it with self._timestamp(); the validation is redundant and misleading since the client value is discarded.
Direct messages addressed to a non-existent recipient_id are silently dropped with no feedback to the sender; send_to has no not-delivered path.
Two convention violations in test_notification_server.py per static analysis: a class not using PascalCase and a module-level constant not UPPER_CASE (convention score 0.82).

strengths: Clean greenfield architecture: single-responsibility NotificationServer class, asyncio-native, lock-protected client registry with uuid client ids.
Solid message validation layer that rejects non-JSON, malformed, and invalid-format payloads with explicit errors to the sender.
Measurably cleaner than the seed: smells -4, duplications 0%, and a net -233/-212 line reduction to a purpose-built ~136 LOC module.
Correctly replaced the irrelevant Flask auth seed rather than bolting WebSocket logic onto it.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured, purpose-built WebSocket notification server that cleanly replaces an unrelated auth-API seed, with only minor issues around client-forgeable system messages, redundant timestamp validation, and silent direct-message delivery failures.

problems.description: Message-type dispatch in `_handle_message` is growing ad hoc: the trailing `else` now silently serves three semantic cases (plain broadcast, system, channel-carrying broadcast), and channel extraction (`_channel_from`) is repeated per branch. The +31 cognitive complexity delta reflects this; a handler-map dispatch would scale better as types multiply.

Conflating channel routing into the broadcast fallback makes the wire protocol ambiguous: a `broadcast` message with a `channel` field is routed to the channel, while an empty/None channel falls through to a global broadcast. Silent fallback can mis-deliver when a client omits `channel` accidentally.

`/channels/{channel}/subscribers` route is parsed via string slicing (`path[len("/channels/") : -len("/subscribers")]`) rather than pattern matching (e.g. regex or a small route table), matching the growth in `process_request`'s if/elif chain — a fragility the new complexity is starting to introduce.

Both SonarQube violations land in the test file (PascalCase and UPPER_CASE rules), likely from the new module-level `get_json` helper rather than fixture-based organization; low severity but recorded by the scanner at convention score 0.82.

strengths: Extracts `_send_to_recipients` shared helper, deduplicating broadcast and channel-broadcast send paths (real DRY improvement over the pre-commit duplication)
`_remove_client` centralizes disconnect cleanup so channel subscriptions are purged on client loss — no stale-subscriber leaks across the three call sites
Defensive URL handling with `urlsplit`/`unquote` plus an empty-channel guard prevents path traversal / malformed-route noise
Complements the code with focused async tests covering subscribe-only delivery, health, and channel endpoints
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped pub/sub feature that refactors cleanly into existing lock/async patterns, though the message-type dispatch and hand-rolled URL parsing are starting to accrue minor complexity debt.

problems.description: SQLiteMessageStore.save/list run blocking sqlite3 I/O directly on the event loop (shared connection with check_same_thread=False). asyncio.Lock serializes calls but does not offload the blocking work, so every accepted message stalls the loop; should use asyncio.to_thread or aiosqlite.
RedisBroker.remove_client strips channel-set memberships but never removes client_id from the 'notifications:clients' hash, leaking stale registry entries.
The 'notifications:clients' hash is written by register_client but never read by any method — dead state that will confuse future maintainers.
NotificationServer.start() performs a non-atomic check-then-act on _listener_task; concurrent first connections can spawn duplicate broker listener tasks.

The two measured convention violations (test_notification_server.py PascalCase / UPPER_CASE) are not part of this diff (only app.py changed); they are pre-existing or from an earlier session and should not be charged to this commit.

strengths: Parameterized SQL throughout the store — no SQL injection surface.
Constructor dependency injection with optional broker/message_store keeps NotificationServer decoupled, testable, and able to degrade gracefully without Redis.
Clean separation of concerns: SQLiteMessageStore and RedisBroker encapsulate persistence and transport while the server stays routing-focused.
Careful lifecycle management — close() cancels the listener task and tears down both store and broker.
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent integration session that adds durable history and cross-instance pub/sub with clean DI and parameterized SQL, held back by synchronous sqlite calls on the event loop and minor registry/bookkeeping leaks — and the two measured convention violations sit in test_notification_server.py, which this diff does not touch.

problems.description: handler() is duck-typed via getattr(self._transport, 'handler', None) with a RuntimeError fallback, but it is not part of the BaseTransport ABC — the server reaches into concrete transport behavior through an ad-hoc seam instead of the abstract interface.

connection: object in the transport interface forces a type: ignore[attr-defined] inside WebSocketTransport.send_message, erasing type safety at the core abstraction boundary; a Protocol or typed connection would preserve it.

_transport_from_environment() lives as a static factory on NotificationServer, coupling the server to concrete transport construction; a standalone factory/registry would keep the server transport-agnostic.

strengths: Clean extraction of connection delivery concerns into BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport via ABC + abstractmethod, genuinely decoupling the server core from WebSocket specifics.
Recipients handling simplified to plain client-id lists, with networked broadcast moved out of NotificationServer and fault isolation (asyncio.gather, return_exceptions) preserved.
Behavior preserved across the refactor: connect/disconnect lifecycle, broker registration, and the system 'connected' message all retained.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound transport-abstraction refactor that improves separation of concerns, with only minor seam-quality blemishes (duck-typed handler, object-typed connection, server-side transport factory); convention score 0.82 matches measurements, and the flagged violations are pre-existing test-file issues outside this diff.

problems.description: The /history branch adds ~26 cognitive complexity to create_process_request, which is already a large if/elif router; extracting per-endpoint handler functions would contain the growth.

_cleanup_expired_messages runs once at startup rather than periodically, so expired messages accumulate for the lifetime of a long-running server despite MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS implying ongoing TTL enforcement.
No test coverage for the new rate-limit path (allow_message / RATE_LIMIT) or the delete_older_than cleanup path.
Two convention violations flagged in test_notification_server.py (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE module constants), per static analysis.

strengths: Extends the existing store/broker layering cleanly: history() and delete_older_than() on the store, allow_message() on the broker.
Fixes a real bug: run_server() now awaits server.start(), which was previously never invoked.
Background cleanup task lifecycle (create_task + await on shutdown + duplicate guard) mirrors the existing _listener_task pattern.
Defensive /history validation (channel required, limit 1-50, ISO timestamp check) matches the existing endpoint style.
Efficient has_more pagination via limit+1 fetch.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive feature commit that fits the existing abstraction cleanly and fixes a real startup bug, but grows the already-monolithic request router and adds a one-shot cleanup task.

compounding_issues: Single-file monolith: all 5 sessions kept app.py monolithic (grew to ~520 LOC), and the HTTP request router in create_process_request accumulated every new endpoint across sessions, becoming increasingly hard to maintain
Synchronous sqlite3 calls on the asyncio event loop in SQLiteMessageStore (noted in S3 review) were never refactored to an executor despite growth of the persistence layer
Dual-bookkeeping of channel state: in-process self._channels and Redis broker sets are maintained in parallel, adding consistency complexity for every subscribe/unsubscribe/disconnect path
Rate limiting only applies when a broker is present (gated on `if self._broker`), so the no-Redis fallback mode silently has no rate limiting
Minor seam blemishes carried forward from S4's refactor: duck-typed transport handler and object-typed connection parameter in BaseTransport
key_decisions: S1: Discarded the irrelevant Flask auth seed entirely and built a purpose-built async WebSocket notification server (~136 LOC) instead of bolting WebSocket logic onto it — a net -233 lines and -4 smells
S2: In-process channel subscription model (dict[channel, set[client_id]]) with HTTP inspection endpoints, centralized _remove_client cleanup to prevent stale-subscriber leaks

S3: Constructor-injected SQLiteMessageStore and RedisBroker, persisting every accepted message and routing via a shared pub/sub channel — enabling cross-instance delivery and graceful degradation without Redis
S4: Extracted BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport ABC to decouple the server core from WebSocket specifics, simplifying recipient handling to plain client-id lists
S5: Redis-backed rate limiting and SQLite TTL-based message cleanup, plus a /history endpoint with has_more pagination — and fixed the previously-never-invoked server.start() bug
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved across the five sessions with no regressions (bugs_delta 0 throughout, 4→10 tests all passing). S1 established a clean, purpose-built foundation; S2 and S3 layered features (channels, persistence, cross-instance pub/sub) at the cost of rising cyclomatic complexity (+31 and +39). S4 was a genuine refactor — extracting the transport abstraction — that reined complexity back to +3 and improved separation of concerns while preserving behavior. S5 delivered cross-cutting features (rate limiting, TTL cleanup, history) and fixed a real startup bug, continuing the established store/broker layering. The arc shows a disciplined agent: build clean, extend, refactor when complexity accumulates, then extend again — the only persistent weakness being the growing monolith and synchronous DB calls.
story_review.summary: An exceptionally coherent five-session story — greenfield, features, integration, refactor, cross-cutting — where each commit builds naturally on the last, quality improved monotonically, and the agent refactored preemptively when complexity accumulated, marred only by a growing single-file monolith and blocking DB calls.
